title: Good stress and bad stress
keyIdea: Stress is your body's alarm. Adrenaline and cortisol make your heart race, your breathing speed up and your muscles tense, ready to act. Short stress that feels like a stretch you can handle, with an end in sight, can help you focus and perform: that is good stress. Stress that is too big, goes on for weeks, or leaves you with no control is bad stress, and it wears down sleep, mood and health. Recovery lets the alarm switch off, and tools like exercise, slow breathing, talking and writing worries down work for real reasons. If stress stops you sleeping or enjoying things for two weeks or more, tell a trusted adult.

kid: Stress is your body's alarm. When something feels hard or scary, your brain sends out two stress hormones, adrenaline and cortisol. Your heart beats faster. You breathe faster. Your muscles get tight. Your stomach slows down, which is the butterflies feeling. Your body is getting ready to fight, run or freeze.

Some stress is good for you. Nerves before a match or a test can make you sharp and focused. This is good stress when the task is a stretch you can handle, it will end soon, and you have some control. Stress turns bad when it is far too big, when it goes on for weeks, or when you feel stuck with no help.

Your body needs time for the alarm to switch off. Sleep, moving your body and talking to a friend all help it calm down. If stress never stops, the alarm stays on. Then you may sleep badly, get headaches, catch colds more often or feel low. Late-night scrolling and energy drinks keep the alarm on.

Good tools work for real reasons. Exercise uses up stress hormones and helps you sleep. A slow breath out, longer than the breath in, slows your heart. Talking shares the load. Writing worries down gets them out of your head. If you cannot sleep or enjoy things for two weeks or more, tell a trusted adult.
adult: This topic helps young people tell helpful stress from harmful stress. Short stress that feels like a manageable challenge often improves focus and performance. Stress that is overwhelming, long lasting or out of the person's control is the kind linked to poor sleep, low mood and illness.

The lab works through five ideas. Learners set off the body's alarm and tap each body part to see what adrenaline does, then turn three dials (size, length and control) to change the same football final from bad stress into good stress. Next they drop recovery into the gaps of a hard week so the stress line can fall back. Then they match coping tools to the reason each one works, and finally they slow a racing heart with long out-breaths.

A common mistake is to think all stress is harmful, so that normal nerves before a test feel like a sign of illness. Another is to judge a coping habit only by how it feels in the moment. Scrolling late at night and energy drinks feel like a break, but they cut sleep and keep the alarm on. Many children also keep stress to themselves for weeks, when two weeks of poor sleep or lost enjoyment is the point to get help.

At home, notice sleep and enjoyment, since both change early when stress builds. Help your child break a big pressure into small steps they can control, and protect time for sleep, exercise and friends during exam season.

familyTip: Before a big event, try the slow breath together: in for four, out for six, three times. Afterwards, ask what helped your child feel ready and what made the nerves worse.

practice.prompt: Before a race, Ana's heart is pounding and her muscles feel tight. What is this?
choices: Her body's alarm getting her ready to run
A sign she is ill
Proof that stress is always bad
practice.hint: Think about what adrenaline does to the heart and muscles.
practice.explain: Adrenaline speeds up the heart and tenses muscles to get the body ready for action. Short stress like this can help her run well.

practice.prompt: Ben has been worried about a problem at home for {n} weeks and can hardly sleep. What kind of stress is this?
choices: Bad stress: it has lasted too long
Good stress: it keeps him alert
Not stress at all
practice.hint: Does the alarm get a chance to switch off?
practice.explain: {n} weeks of worry with poor sleep means the alarm never switches off. That is bad stress, and he should talk to a trusted adult.

practice.prompt: Why does a slow breath help when you feel stressed?
choices: A long breath out slows your heart down
It makes you fall asleep
It stops stress hormones forever
practice.hint: Which part of the breath should be longer?
practice.explain: Breathing out slowly, for longer than you breathe in, slows your heart rate and helps the alarm calm down.

practice.prompt: Kai has a test in {d} days and feels he can do it if he revises a little each day. What kind of stress is this?
choices: Good stress: a stretch he can handle with an end in sight
Bad stress: he should skip the test
No stress at all
practice.hint: Is it too big, too long or out of his control?
practice.explain: A test in {d} days that feels doable, with a plan he controls, is good stress. It can help him focus.

practice.prompt: After a stressful day, which helps the alarm switch off?
choices: A walk and a good night's sleep
An energy drink
Scrolling on a phone until 1 am
practice.hint: Which choice helps you recover and sleep?
practice.explain: Moving your body uses up stress hormones and sleep lets them fall back. Caffeine and late screens keep the alarm on.

pool.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be good stress?
choices: Nerves before a school play you have practised for
Worry about money at home that lasts months
Being bullied every day
pool.hint: Good stress is short and feels like a stretch you can handle.
pool.explain: Nerves before a practised play are short and manageable, so they can help you perform. The others last too long or are out of your control.

pool.prompt: Zara has felt too stressed to enjoy anything for {n} weeks. What should she do?
choices: Tell a trusted adult and get help
Keep it to herself and push on
Drink energy drinks to keep going
pool.explain: {n} weeks without enjoyment is past the two-week point, so it is time to tell a parent, teacher or doctor.

pool.prompt: Why does exercise help with stress?
choices: It uses up stress hormones and helps you sleep
It only makes you too tired to worry
It does not help at all
pool.hint: Think about what happens to stress hormones and to sleep.
pool.explain: Exercise lowers stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol, and it helps you sleep better, which helps you recover.

pool.prompt: When the stress alarm goes off, what happens to digestion?
choices: It slows down
It speeds up
It stops for a whole day
pool.hint: Where does the body send its energy when it is ready to act?
pool.explain: Digestion slows so that blood and energy can go to the muscles. That is why stress can feel like butterflies.

pool.prompt: Leo has {k} pieces of homework due and feels swamped. Which step gives him back some control?
choices: List them and start the smallest one
Leave them all until the night before
Ignore them and play games
pool.hint: Which choice turns one big pressure into small steps?
pool.explain: Listing all {k} tasks and starting the smallest one turns a big pressure into steps he controls, which makes the stress easier to handle.

pool.prompt: Why can writing your worries down help?
choices: It gets them out of your head so you can sort them
It makes the problems vanish
It only helps if nobody reads it
pool.hint: What happens to worries that just go round and round in your head?
pool.explain: Writing worries down moves them out of your head, so you can see them clearly and plan what to do.

pool.prompt: Which pattern is worst for your body?
choices: Medium stress that never lets up for weeks
One scary moment on a rollercoaster
Nerves before a race
pool.hint: Which one gives the alarm no time to switch off?
pool.explain: Stress that never lets up keeps the alarm on, which wears down sleep, mood and health. Short scares pass.

pool.prompt: Which breath calms you down most?
choices: Slow, with the breath out longer than the breath in
Fast and deep
Holding your breath as long as you can
pool.hint: Fast breathing is what the alarm does.
pool.explain: A slow breath with a longer out-breath slows the heart. Fast breathing and holding your breath keep you tense.

visual.caption: Good stress or bad stress? Ask: is it too big, too long, or out of my control?

items: A test you have revised for
Giving a short talk in class

lab.caption: Flagship lab: set off the body's alarm, dial bad stress into good, let the alarm switch off, and breathe your heart rate down.
